<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<p id="id1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">in Machine Learning</span></p>
<p id="id1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:298%;">Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations</span></p>
<p id="id1.8" class="ltx_p">submitted by</p>
<p id="id1.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:144%;">Joschka Braun</span></p>
<p id="id1.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">joschka.braun@student.uni-tuebingen.de</span></p>
<p id="id1.11" class="ltx_p">Supervisors and Examiners:</p>
<p id="id1.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">Ph.D. Seyed Ali Bahrainian</span></p>
<p id="id1.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">Prof. Michael Franke</span></p>
<p id="id1.14" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">Prof. Carsten Eickhoff</span></p>
<p id="id1.15" class="ltx_p"><span id="id1.15.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">Tübingen, June 12, 2025</span></p>
</div>
<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Steering vectors are a lightweight method for controlling language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although effective on average, steering effect sizes vary across samples and are unreliable for many target behaviors. In my thesis, I investigate why steering reliability differs across behaviors and how it is impacted by steering vector training data. First, I find that higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering. Second, I observe that behavior datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated along the steering direction are more reliably steerable. Finally, steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct, yet perform similarly well and exhibit correlated efficacy across datasets. My findings suggest that steering vectors are unreliable when the latent target behavior representation is not effectively approximated by the linear steering direction. Taken together, these insights offer a practical diagnostic for steering unreliability and motivate the development of more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>The rise of foundation models and the need for post-training adaptation</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Over the last decade of Artificial Intelligence (AI) research, a significant paradigm shift from developing task-specific models towards training large-scale foundation models occurred <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bommasani et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Foundation models are pre-trained on extensive and diverse datasets, typically leveraging generic, self-supervised training objectives rather than focusing on narrow downstream applications. For example, in Natural Language Processing (NLP), state-of-the-art Language Models (LMs), which often use the Transformer architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, are trained on next token prediction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bengio et al., 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">GemmaTeam, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Llama3Team, 2024</a>)</cite>. During training with this generic training objective, broad capabilities emerge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020b</a>)</cite>. Similarly, in Computer Vision, architectures such as Vision Transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and models like CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> learn broad visual representations from vast image collections, often through self-supervised tasks like contrastive learning or image completion, before adaptation to specific recognition or generation tasks. This generalist pre-training facilitates the learning of powerful, transferable representations of relevant concepts. The learned representations can then be leveraged for specific downstream tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devlin et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Foundation models are increasingly deployed across a wide array of applications and diverse user groups, such as through interactive chat systems or educational tools <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bommasani et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kasneci et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ray, 2023</a>)</cite>. However, without specific adaptation, their deployment performance in these specific contexts is often suboptimal, as generic outputs may not adequately address task constraints or cater to individual user preferences. Consequently, adapting foundation models to specific applications and users has driven research into post-training and inference-time methods for adapting and personalizing foundation model outputs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Post-training adaptations to foundation models</h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Approaches to control and adapt pre-trained foundation language models can be categorized into three main strategies: fine-tuning methods that update model parameters, prompt engineering techniques that guide the model via its input, and inference-time control mechanisms that shape the generation process dynamically.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-tuning approaches learn updates to model parameters during a post-training phase. This includes techniques like supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for instruction following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022a</a>)</cite>, preference optimization through methods such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christiano et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) such as with adapters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Houlsby et al., 2019</a>)</cite> and Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> that reduce computational costs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt engineering approaches leverage in-context learning (ICL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to steer model behavior by carefully designing input prompts or tuning them algorithmically without altering model weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shin et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lester et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. This ranges from providing zero-shot or few-shot examples to guide task performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020a</a>)</cite> to employing more complex strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to elicit step-by-step reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022c</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Inference-time control mechanisms dynamically shape outputs during the generation process. These include modifying decoding algorithms, for instance, through techniques like nucleus sampling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Holtzman et al., 2020</a>)</cite> to control output randomness or directly reweighting logits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Braun et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>, Plug and Play Language Models (PPLM) that use attribute models to steer generation towards desired characteristics by modifying hidden states during inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dathathri et al., 2020</a>)</cite> or applying external guidance mechanisms such as Classifier-Free Guidance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho and Salimans, 2022</a>)</cite> to more strongly adhere to desired attributes.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.3 </span>Activation Engineering</h3>

<div id="S1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on these approaches, Activation Engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, also called Representation Engineering  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, is an interpretability-inspired paradigm focused on controlling model outputs. Activation Engineering methods leverage empirical observations about the structure of learned representations to modify activations during text generation. By intervening at the level of learned model representations, interventions might be more robust and generalize better across contexts, than interventions that treat the model as a black box.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.4 </span>Steering vectors</h3>

<div id="S1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the field of Activation Engineering, a family of methods called steering vectors has been especially prominent. Steering vectors leverage the observation that many human-interpretable behaviors and concepts like truthfulness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark, 2024</a>)</cite>, refusal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and sentiment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Konen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> are represented as linear directions in models’ activation spaces. Modifying activations along that direction results in changes of the expression of the given behavior.
Steering vector methods such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> control LLM behavior simply by adding a learned bias to the residual stream activations during inference. Steering interventions are appealing because they usually require less data than conventional fine-tuning, do not change model parameters, and are computationally cheap to apply at test time. Like fine-tuning, Activation Engineering methods can be combined with prompt engineering approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.5 </span>Limitations of steering vectors</h3>

<div id="S1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite demonstrations of efficacy in constrained settings, such as multiple-choice benchmarks and simplified tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Todd et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendel et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krasheninnikov and Krueger, 2024</a>)</cite>, steering methods exhibit notable limitations when subjected to a more thorough evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pres et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brumley et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Braun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A central issue is the variability of the per-sample steering effect size. While steering vectors demonstrate net-positive impacts on average for many target behaviors, the steering impact is often inconsistent, negligible, or even counterproductive on some samples  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brumley et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> report that steering reliability significantly depends on the dataset and the behavior being steered, with some remaining unsteerable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, applying steering vectors with high steering strengths can degrade text quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stickland et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Steering vectors also struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios where vectors are applied in contexts different from their extraction, such as due to prompt changes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Consequently, these critical issues of inconsistent efficacy and unreliable generalization hinder the widespread adoption of steering methods in real-world applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.6 </span>Research questions</h3>

<div id="S1.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The documented limitations in steering vector efficacy, particularly their variable reliability, motivate the central inquiries of this thesis. My thesis aims to address the following research questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">What are the underlying factors in model activation patterns that contribute to the observed variability in CAA steering vector reliability across different datasets and target behaviors?</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Can the training process of CAA steering vectors be modified to produce more consistently reliable control over language model behavior?</span></p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.7 </span>Research scope</h3>

<div id="S1.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I evaluate CAA steering vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>)</cite> on 36 binary-choice datasets about language model assistant behavior and personality by  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al. (2022)</a></cite>, for which previous work finds that CAA steering with the Llama 2-7B-Chat model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> performs well for some datasets but not others <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.8 </span>Thesis contributions</h3>

<div id="S1.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This thesis makes the following contributions to understanding the reliability of steering vectors in language models:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S1.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Identifying geometric predictors of steering vector reliability:</span>
Addressing the question of <span id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">why</span> steering vectors exhibit variable reliability, my thesis investigates the underlying activation patterns and demonstrates that:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2.i1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Directional agreement</span> within the training data, quantified by the cosine similarity between activation differences and the resulting steering vector, is a significant predictor of the subsequent steering vector’s success. Higher directional agreement in the training activations is predictive for more reliable steering.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S1.I2.i1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">separability</span> of positive and negative example activations along the learned steering vector direction serves as both a conceptual explanation and an empirical predictor for steering efficacy. Better separation implies a more distinct representation of the target behavior, leading to more reliable interventions.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluating the impact of training data on steering vector reliability:</span>
To investigate how different training prompt types impact the resulting training activations and steering vectors, I systematically compare seven training prompt types against each other:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2.i2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Different <span id="S1.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">prompt types</span> generate directionally distinct steering vectors for the same target behavior. Despite these differences, their overall performance is similar, and their reliability and efficacy is correlated across datasets.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S1.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">My findings suggest that CAA steering vector unreliability is caused by fundamental mismatch: its simple, linear function class is too restrictive to effectively approximate the often non-linear latent target behavior representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the background section, I explain how language models process and represent text, and how steering methods can manipulate internal representations to influence model behavior. I begin by outlining the development of word embeddings, detailing their progression from sparse to dense, and from static to contextual embeddings. This development is crucial because it first revealed emergent linear representations within embedding spaces and demonstrated the viability of vector arithmetic. Next, I detail the transformer architecture, explaining how its layer-dependent representation spaces differ from word embedding spaces. Building on this, I introduce the Linear Representation Hypothesis, explaining its meaning alongside the evidence for and against its validity. Subsequently, I introduce the field of Activation Engineering with a focus on steering methods, which are inspired by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. I will then cover their documented shortcomings, including the unreliability of steering effects, and outline common hypotheses for these failures, connecting these directly to the transformer representation space structure. Through this comprehensive overview, I provide the necessary context for my thesis’s investigation into why steering vectors are unreliable.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Learned word embeddings</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Word embeddings, or word representations, are a type of feature representation that map words and phrases from a vocabulary to real-valued vectors in an embedding or representation space. The primary objective is to capture semantic meanings of words, such that words with similar meanings or contextual roles are represented by similar vectors in the embedding space. Most word embedding methods are based on the <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Distributional Hypothesis</span>, which states that words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Harris, 1954</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sahlgren, 2008</a>)</cite>. Early approaches typically used <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">sparse representations</span> for words, such as one-hot encodings or count-based methods like Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luhn, 1958</a>)</cite>. While straightforward, these representations are generally very high-dimensional with many zero values and fail to capture nuanced semantic relationships effectively <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le and Mikolov, 2014</a>)</cite>. In contrast, modern neural word embedding methods learn more compact <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dense representations</span>, which are lower-dimensional continuous vectors. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bengio et al. (2003)</a></cite> showed that jointly learning dense word vectors with a neural language model mitigates the curse of dimensionality. Dense representations also empirically result in richer encodings of semantic information and vector directions that often represent latent features of the represented words <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bengio et al., 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.1 </span>Dense word embedding methods</h4>

<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Word2Vec</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al. (2013a)</a></cite> introduce Word2Vec, a neural network which learns dense, distributed word embeddings by predicting words from their local contexts. Word2Vec uses two architectures: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW), which predicts a target word from its surrounding words, and Skip-Gram, which does the reverse and predicts the surrounding words from a target word. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al. (2013b)</a></cite> further developed Word2Vec by including common multi-word phrases and hierarchical softmax. The resulting embeddings capture semantic relationships like synonyms, antonyms, and analogies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013c</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Global Vectors for Word Representation (GloVe)</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al. (2014)</a></cite> introduce the GloVe model, which learns word representations based on global word-word co-occurrence statistics from a training corpus. GloVe factorizes a matrix of these statistics, aiming to combine the benefits of global matrix factorization methods with the local context window advantages of Word2Vec.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FastText</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bojanowski et al. (2017)</a></cite> introduce FastText, which improves upon Word2Vec by representing each word as a bag of character n-gram to include subword information. This allows it to generate embeddings for out-of-vocabulary words, and often performs better for morphologically rich languages.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers (BERT)</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devlin et al. (2019)</a></cite> introduce BERT, which brought about a significant change in word representations by focusing on <span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">contextual embeddings</span> using the Transformer architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. Compared to the <span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">static embeddings</span> from previous embedding models, which embed words identically irrespective of the surrounding context, contextual models produce different embeddings for the same word depending on its usage, thereby capturing polysemy and more complex linguistic context.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.2 </span>Limitations of static embeddings compared to contextual embeddings</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While static embeddings can encode various concepts including gender, tense, language, or geographical information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2014</a>)</cite>, they lack contextual information to resolve polysemanticity and cannot meaningfully represent higher-level concepts such as truthfulness or bias. Although many words might be associated with certain properties, associations cannot be certain without context. In Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.1.2 Limitations of static embeddings compared to contextual embeddings ‣ 2.1 Learned word embeddings ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> I list examples in which static embeddings can be misleading and contextual embeddings help to more accurately represent the words.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S2.T1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S2.T1.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">

</span></td>

<tr id="S2.T1.3.3" class="ltx_tr">

</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:318.7pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">He called me an <span id="S2.T1.3.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">idiot</span>, but he was just joking.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.3.4" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="S2.T1.3.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Bias</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:318.7pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">They hired her because she’s a <span id="S2.T1.3.4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">woman</span>.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.3.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.3.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:54.1pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Tense</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:318.7pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">He will <span id="S2.T1.3.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">go</span> to the meeting, I <span id="S2.T1.3.5.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">go</span> to every week.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.3.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.3.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:54.1pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Truthfulness</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.6.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:318.7pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The world is <span id="S2.T1.3.6.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">flat</span>.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.3.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.3.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.7.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:54.1pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Lexical Ambiguity</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:318.7pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Words such as <span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ring</span>, <span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">lie</span>, <span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spring</span>, <span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">leaves</span>, and <span id="S2.T1.3.7.2.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bank</span> exhibit polysemy, possessing multiple distinct meanings contingent upon their contextual usage.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.3.8" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.3.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.8.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:54.1pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Cross-Linguistic Homographs</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S2.T1.3.8.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:318.7pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.3.8.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">words like <span id="S2.T1.3.8.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bald</span>, <span id="S2.T1.3.8.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">fast</span>, <span id="S2.T1.3.8.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rat</span>, and <span id="S2.T1.3.8.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gift</span> represent identical input tokens (orthographically) that should map to divergent semantic representations depending on the specific language context (e.g., English versus German)</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S2.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Examples where static word embeddings lack crucial context information to adequately represent a text property. The local context could disambiguate the text properties and make contextual embeddings superior to static embeddings in such cases.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Transformer architecture</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Transformer architecture, introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al. (2017)</a></cite>, uses <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dense contextual embeddings</span> to represent input text. An input sequence is typically passed through the following key processing stages within a Transformer model. My mathematical notation is based on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phuong and Hutter (2022)</a></cite> and can be found in more detail in the Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Mathematical Notation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 1: Tokenization</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The input text is segmented into tokens <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> - which may be words, sub-words, or characters - using a tokenizer, often pre-trained on a large corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sennrich et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib105" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. These tokens form the model’s vocabulary <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>. Each token is mapped to a unique token ID <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in[\mathbb{N}_{V}]:=\{1,\ldots,\mathbb{N}_{V}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in[\mathbb{N}_{V}]:=\{1,\ldots,\mathbb{N}_{V}\}</annotation></semantics></math> from the model’s vocabulary, translating human-readable text into natural numbers <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, the word “cat” might be tokenized into the token ID 1777 using a tokenizer. This discrete representation enables the subsequent numerical processing performed by the model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 2: Token embedding</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Token IDs are mapped to fixed-size dense vector embeddings <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> in a high-dimensional representation space <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>. These embeddings, learned during training, encode semantic and syntactic properties of the tokens. For instance, token ID 1777 might be mapped to a vector <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.41,\ldots,0.97]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.41</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0.97</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.41,\ldots,0.97]</annotation></semantics></math>. This mapping from token IDs (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>) to vectors (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>) is done by an embedding matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\mathbb{N}_{V}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\mathbb{N}_{V}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which effectively acts as a lookup table. Additionally, positional information is incorporated through the positional embedding matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\tau_{\text{max}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\tau_{\text{max}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 3: Transformations by the Transformer</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The initial embedding vector <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> is iteratively processed through multiple Transformer layers. Each layer applies attention mechanisms, non-linear activation functions, and layer normalization. The vector’s dimensionality <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> typically remains constant. Conceptually, each layer transforms its input vector by incorporating contextual information from other tokens in the sequence, capturing complex inter-token dependencies. This process results in a contextually enriched output vector <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 4: Prediction head</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prediction head converts the final contextual output vector <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> into a probability distribution over the model’s entire vocabulary <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>. This distribution signifies the likelihood of each token being the next in the sequence. For instance, an output vector <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1.17,\ldots,0.37]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>1.17</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0.37</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1.17,\ldots,0.37]</annotation></semantics></math> is passed through a linear layer and a softmax function to generate probabilities for tokens like “sleeps” or “jumps.” Mathematically, this transforms <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> via a linear projection with a weight matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}_{V}\times d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}_{V}\times d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> to produce logits, which a softmax function then transforms into a probability distribution over the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}_{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}_{V}</annotation></semantics></math> vocabulary tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 5: Sampling and token translation</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the generated probability distribution, a token ID is selected, often by choosing the most probable token (greedy decoding) or by employing other sampling strategies. This selected token ID is then converted back into its human-readable token representation. For example, if token ID 1998 is selected, it might correspond to the word “sleeps.” This stage maps the probability distribution over the vocabulary (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{|V|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{|V|}</annotation></semantics></math>) to a specific token ID (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>), which is subsequently translated into human-readable text. This mapping from the model’s internal numerical predictions back to human language completes one generation step. The generation steps can be repeated autoregressively, meaning the just-generated token is used as input to the model to help predict the subsequent token, allowing for the generation of entire sequences.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Representation space of Transformer-based language models</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How information is represented and transformed within individual Transformer layers is an active area of research that includes different approaches and nomenclature  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hernandez et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Engels et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordás et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. I will introduce key terms describing representation spaces and the results and current hypothesis that are most relevant to studying the reliability of steering vectors.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.3.1 </span>Key terms describing representation spaces</h4>

<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Representation space:</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the context of deep learning models, particularly Transformers, the representation space, also known as the activation space or hidden state space, is a high-dimensional vector space <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> where each input token <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is initially mapped to a vector representation <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>. These vectors are then propagated and transformed through the model’s layers. The structure of the representation spaces at different model layers determines how the encoded information is stored, manipulated, and retrieved.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Features:</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Distinct concepts, attributes, behaviors, or characteristics that are encoded in the representation space. Features can capture syntactic information (e.g., part of speech), semantic content (e.g., sentiment, topic), or abstract notions (e.g., truthfulness, simplicity). Empirically, features often correspond to directions <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> in the representation space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Linear directions:</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A feature is often represented as a normalized vector direction <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the direction encodes the feature, and the magnitude along that direction encodes the strength of the feature. In some cases, features may correspond to a subspace <math id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>, spanned by multiple feature vectors.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:144.9pt;">
<div id="S2.F1.fig1.3" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:186.3pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17881v1/king-man+woman=queen.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:257/195;" width="257" height="195"></object>
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.fig1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The hypothetical representation space illustrates how features like gender and royalty can be represented as linear directions. The representation of “king” for instance, can be decomposed into its components along the “male” and “royal” direction within this subspace. This linear structure enables vector arithmetic operations such as analogies (e.g., “king” - “man” + “woman” <math id="S2.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math> “queen”) through vector addition and scalar multiplication. Such representation vector arithmetics, using linearly encoded features, were first demonstrated by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al. (2013a)</a></cite> in their work on Word2Vec</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.3.2 </span>Properties of Transformer representation spaces</h4>

</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Representations are layer-dependent</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Feature representations within Transformers are layer-dependent. Early layers often capture more syntactic and local semantic information, such as grammar, sentiment, and basic word-sense disambiguation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tenney et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hewitt and Liang, 2019</a>)</cite>. In contrast, middle and later layers tend to build more abstract, context-rich representations, integrating information across longer distances to capture higher-level semantic information and even some forms of factual or commonsense knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rogers et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. This hierarchical processing is conceptually similar to how CNNs learn features, progressing from simple to complex patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeiler and Fergus, 2014</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite this hierarchical transformation, there is evidence that certain directional information within the representation space can generalize across layers. Residual connections play a crucial role here by allowing subsequent layers to refine existing representations rather than learning entirely new ones, thus promoting some consistency in how features are encoded directionally <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Voita et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> show that feature directions, once identified, can maintain their meaning across different layers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Representations learned by AI models might not be easily human-interpretable</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although AI models, particularly LLMs, are trained on vast amounts of human-written text and human-generated data, their learned internal representations do not necessarily align with familiar human concepts or are easily decomposable into familiar concepts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipton, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. The depth and complexity of deep learning models creates “black-box” mechanisms that defy straightforward explanation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rudin, 2019</a>)</cite>.
Evidence from reinforcement learning highlights this divergence. For instance, AlphaZero, which mastered games like chess, shogi, and Go through self-play without human priors, developed concepts and strategies unfamiliar to human experts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">McGrath et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silver et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. These novel representations, while effective, demonstrate that AI can optimize solutions in ways that deviate significantly from human conceptual frameworks  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Furthermore, the notion of “human interpretability” itself is complex, as concepts and the way the world is structured can vary across different human cultures and languages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gleitman and Papafragou, 2011</a>; <a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nisbett, 2003</a>)</cite>. This inherent diversity in human cognition suggests that even if AI representations captured some human-like concepts, they might not be universally understood or could be biased toward the dominant conceptualizations within the training data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consequently, while the internal representations of LLMs undoubtedly possess structure, this structure may not align neatly with established human concepts. It is plausible that LLMs develop novel, emergent abstractions or utilize conceptual frameworks that we currently lack or find challenging to recognize, making their internal workings difficult to fully decipher even when their outputs are coherent  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>. The quest to understand these representations often involves developing specialized techniques to probe and translate model behavior into terms that are meaningful to humans <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carter et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Linear Representation Hypothesis</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) states that neural networks represent many features as linear directions. Variants of the LRH are stated across a wide range of empirical studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alain and Bengio, 2018</a>)</cite>, from early word-embedding literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2014</a>)</cite> to more recent work on language model interpretability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Engels et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark, 2024</a>)</cite>. Although authors use different names like “vector arithmetic”, “semantic directions”, “neuronal subspaces” or simply “linear probes”, they all point to the same broad observation:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Human-interpretable features often correspond to
<br class="ltx_break">approximately linear subspaces in the learned representation spaces.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This claim is the basis for steering vectors. If a feature is encoded by a single direction, then adding, subtracting, or otherwise manipulating that direction provides a direct handle for controllable generation and interpretability. Understanding when the LRH holds and when it breaks determines how reliable such steering interventions can be. The LRH has a weak and a strong version:</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weak Linear Representation Hypothesis:</h5>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some features are approximately encoded as linear directions <math id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}</annotation></semantics></math> in the representation space.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Strong Linear Representation Hypothesis:</h5>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All or the vast majority of features are encoded as linear directions <math id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}</annotation></semantics></math> in the representation space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The notion that a feature is represented by a <span id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">linear direction</span> might satisfy several progressively stronger properties:</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linearity:</span> The feature correlates with projection onto <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}</annotation></semantics></math>. for some contexts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Universality (Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS1" title="2.4.1 Universality of feature directions ‣ 2.4 Linear Representation Hypothesis ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.1</span></a>):</span> The same <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}</annotation></semantics></math> applies across contexts and even languages.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scalability (Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS2" title="2.4.2 Scalability: Feature strength is encoded by magnitude ‣ 2.4 Linear Representation Hypothesis ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.2</span></a>):</span> The feature strength varies monotonically with the magnitude <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}=\alpha\hat{\mathbf{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}=\alpha\hat{\mathbf{f}}</annotation></semantics></math>, enabling continuous control.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Disentanglement (Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS3" title="2.4.3 Orthogonality and entanglement of feature directions ‣ 2.4 Linear Representation Hypothesis ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.3</span></a>):</span> Different feature directions are orthogonal, so changing one leaves the others untouched.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decomposability:</span> A representation can be decomposed into linearly independent atomic features.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These criteria are idealized. In practice, directions can drift across layers or languages, magnitudes may saturate, and orthogonality is rarely perfect. Still, partial satisfaction is often enough for steering.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.1 </span>Universality of feature directions</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A feature direction <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}</annotation></semantics></math> is universal if it points in the same way regardless of the context or language in which it appears. Classic word embedding analogies illustrate this:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{actor}-\text{actress}\;\approx\;\text{husband}-\text{wife}\;\approx\;\text{man}-\text{woman}\;\approx\;\text{Mann}-\text{Frau}\;\approx\;\text{homme}-\text{femme}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>actor</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>actress</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><mtext>husband</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>wife</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><mtext>man</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>woman</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><mtext>Mann</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>Frau</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><mtext>homme</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>femme</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{actor}-\text{actress}\;\approx\;\text{husband}-\text{wife}\;\approx\;\text{man}-\text{woman}\;\approx\;\text{Mann}-\text{Frau}\;\approx\;\text{homme}-\text{femme}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Universality tolerates scale differences, e.g. “actor” – “actress” may project to a smaller magnitude than “man” – “woman”, but demands directional stability. Universality is desirable because steering vectors can generalize across contexts, whereas non-universal feature directions would necessitate context-dependent controls.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.2 </span>Scalability: Feature strength is encoded by magnitude</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A learned feature direction <math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1}</annotation></semantics></math> not only represents the presence of a feature, it also encodes the strength with which it is present. Any activation <math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}</annotation></semantics></math> can be decomposed into an orthogonal component and a component aligned with the feature,
<math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}_{\perp}+\alpha\hat{\mathbf{f}},\quad\alpha(\mathbf{z})=\langle\mathbf{z},\hat{\mathbf{f}}\rangle," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}_{\perp}+\alpha\hat{\mathbf{f}},\quad\alpha(\mathbf{z})=\langle\mathbf{z},\hat{\mathbf{f}}\rangle,</annotation></semantics></math>
where the scalar projection <math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> functions as a continuous measure of feature strength.
For features that have an ordinal ranking like size or sentiment moving along the positive or negative direction therefore scales the expressed feature in a predictable, continuous manner. Scalability might saturate beyond a model-dependent <math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> where additional movement yields little semantic change. For categorical features that lack ordinal structure like languages or animals the meaning of magnitude might be different.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17881v1/sentiment-scale.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/80;" width="476" height="80"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17881v1/size-scale.svg" id="S2.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/80;" width="476" height="80"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Linear scaling of sentiment and object size along their respective feature directions.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Scalability of feature strength allows for continuous changes in meaning by moving incrementally along the direction encoding the feature. For steering vectors this means fine-grained and predictable steering of the feature expression is possible. If changing a representation along a feature direction substantially changes the meaning, at least fine-grained steering would not be possible.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.3 </span>Orthogonality and entanglement of feature directions</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If directions of different features <math id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> are not orthogonal, they are entangled. In such cases, changing the representation along one feature direction <math id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> will also change feature 2. Only if <math id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{1},\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{2}\rangle=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{1},\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{2}\rangle=0</annotation></semantics></math>, they can be changed independently.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In word embeddings, spurious correlations between feature directions are common.
