For instance, the gender direction is often entangled with other professional features (see Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.4.3 Orthogonality and entanglement of feature directions ‣ 2.4 Linear Representation Hypothesis ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bolukbasi et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ethayarajh et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Examples for this are “programmer” - “man” + “woman” <math id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math> “homemaker” and “doctor” - “man” + “woman” <math id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math> “nurse”. Similar entanglements were found in language models, where steering towards positive sentiment simultaneously lowers refusal rates for harmful user requests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F3.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17881v1/gender_professional_position_entanglement.svg" id="S2.F3.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/476;" width="476" height="476"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S2.F3.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Gender and professional position are entangled.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F3.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17881v1/gender_professional_position_disentangled.svg" id="S2.F3.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/476;" width="476" height="476"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S2.F3.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Gender and professional position are disentangled</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Because of feature entanglement in (a), changing the gender also changes the professional position. For disentangled features, gender and professional positions can be varied independently.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Entanglement is undesirable, as steering one feature impacts unrelated features. Some entanglement might be inherent to the features, like entanglement between sentiment and toxicity, because toxic text usually has negative sentiment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.4 </span>Evidence and reasons for and against the Linear Representation Hypothesis</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The case in favor of the LRH is based on several recurring observations. Neural networks use many affine transformations, so features that align with linear directions can be manipulated with minimal distortion, possibly resulting in an inductive bias toward linear representations. Additionally, regular renormalization via layer normalization might incentivize features to be represented as directions, to stay robust to normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krasheninnikov and Krueger, 2024</a>)</cite>. Empirically, linear probes repeatedly isolate single vectors that predict sentiment, gender, truthfulness, refusal, and other features, and causal interventions along those vectors reliably modulate the corresponding behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alain and Bengio, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Nonetheless, a growing body of counter-evidence shows that linearity is neither universal nor guaranteed. Controlled experiments with recurrent networks and reduced-scale LLMs reveal “onion-like” axes whose inner and outer shells denote qualitatively different classes rather than graded intensity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordás et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. As model capacity and the number of tracked concepts increase, layer normalization and superposition effects encourage representations in which multiple features share a direction or split across curved manifolds, contradicting the strong LRH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Engels et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, the strong claim that all features are encoded as linear, universal, scalable, disentangled directions is almost certainly false for Transformer-based language models. However, abundant evidence indicates that some human-interpretable features can be approximated by linear directions and often satisfy monotonic scaling over a useful range. These partial successes justify continued use of linear analyses while motivating complementary methods for the many cases where linearity breaks down.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5 </span>Activation Engineering</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Activation Engineering aims to understand how features are represented in model activations and to leverage this for targeted control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. It builds on earlier interpretability work, such as using linear probes to demonstrate that intermediate layers learn increasingly separable features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alain and Bengio, 2018</a>)</cite>. Activation Engineering extends ideas developed for word embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2013a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2014</a>)</cite> to layer-level representations in neural models. However, studying these layer specific representations introduces new challenges, as changes to a layer cannot directly be mapped to the human-interpretable token space. For word embeddings, the inverse embedding matrix can be applied, but in neural networks, many non-linear transformations are applied to a layer activation before an output token is generated. Nevertheless, techniques like SelfIE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> allow generating natural language descriptions of internal model activations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.5.1 </span>Representation Engineering vs Mechanistic Interpretability</h4>

<div id="S2.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Representation Engineering and Mechanistic Interpretability both aim to improve our scientific understanding of neural networks and to create tools to monitor and control them. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al. (2023)</a></cite> describe Representation Engineering as a top-down approach that focuses on understanding and manipulating model representations. Mechanical Interpretability, on the other hand, seeks to reverse-engineer neural networks by studying single neurons and circuits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Important findings from Mechanistic Interpretability are that hidden unit activations in CNNs can correspond to human-interpretable features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bau et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Another important finding is the Superposition Hypothesis, that neural networks represent more concepts than dimensions by taking so-called superpositions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.6 </span>Steering methods</h3>

<div id="S2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Steering methods are a family of Activation Engineering methods that steer model behavior by modifying the model activations <math id="S2.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> during inference. The core idea is to apply a learned transformation, or mapping function <math id="S2.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{feature}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>feature</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{feature}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>, to these activations at given model layers. This transformation is designed to specifically change how an encoded feature <math id="S2.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math> is expressed, ideally influencing the model’s generated text in a desired way while preserving other information within the representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A primary challenge in developing such feature steering methods is selecting an appropriate function class <math id="S2.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{feature}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>feature</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{feature}}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the high-dimensional representation spaces <math id="S2.SS6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> of current language models (often with <math id="S2.SS6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{e}&gt;1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{e}&gt;1000</annotation></semantics></math>), the “curse of dimensionality” is a significant concern. A highly flexible function class might offer low approximation error and have the capacity to represent the true, ideal transformation accurately. However, it simultaneously risks high estimation error, as numerous complex functions could fit the limited training data well but fail to generalize well both in and out of distribution due to overfitting. Conversely, a too simple function class, like a basic bias offset, might exhibit low estimation error but suffer from high approximation error if the required representation transformation is more complex. Consequently, carefully selecting the class of possible mapping functions, <math id="S2.SS6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{feature}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>feature</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{feature}}</annotation></semantics></math>, is crucial to strike an optimal trade-off between approximation and estimation errors such that the transformation accurately targets and modifies the intended feature, learns efficiently from the available data, and generalizes robustly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Steering methods differ primarily in the function class they choose for <math id="S2.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{feature}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>feature</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{feature}}</annotation></semantics></math> (ranging from simple bias offsets to more complex affine transformations) and their optimization objective (such as matching distributional means or covariances, or minimizing a specific loss function). Despite these variations in methodology, most approaches tend to use similar types of training data to learn the steering function <math id="S2.SS6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{feature}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>feature</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{feature}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.6.1 </span>Training data for steering methods</h4>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most steering methods learn the steering intervention from a dataset of paired samples. One sample elicits the target feature or behavior, whereas the other sample elicits the opposite or absence of the target feature or behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{n}^{+},\mathbf{x}_{n}^{-})\mid n\in[\mathbb{N}_{\text{train}}]\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{n}^{+},\mathbf{x}_{n}^{-})\mid n\in[\mathbb{N}_{\text{train}}]\}</annotation></semantics></math> be the steering vector training dataset, where <math id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{n}^{+}\in V^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{n}^{+}\in V^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the <math id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-th positive example and <math id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{n}^{-}\in V^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{n}^{-}\in V^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the <math id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-th negative example for the feature. Each example is a sequence of tokens and <math id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the total number of training samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al. (2023)</a></cite> use free-form text samples as training data to elicit and extract the target behaviors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Free-form sentiment training sample</h4>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_tabbing">
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#228B22;">Positive sentiment example</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Negative sentiment example</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">I am happy today because it is sunny.</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">I am not happy today because it is raining.</span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> use multiple-choice whose different answers showcase the target behavior. Because multiple choice questions can be used more easily for evaluation of steering effect size, and can more easily be generated symmetrically, they are often preferred <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Multiple-choice question sentiment training sample</h4>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_tabbing">
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#228B22;">Positive (+) example of behavior</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Negative (-) example of behavior</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[INST] Are you feeling happy today?</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[INST] Are you feeling happy today?</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Choices:</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Choices:</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(A) Yes</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(A) Yes</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(B) No</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.5.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(B) No</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[/INST]</span> <span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(<span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#228B22;">A</span>)</span></td>
<td id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[/INST]</span> <span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(<span id="S2.SS6.SSSx2.p1.1.6.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">B</span>)</span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.6.2 </span>Specific steering methods</h4>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early work on steering methods includes<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramani et al. (2022)</a></cite>, who optimized randomly initialized additive vectors through gradient descent to generate target sentences. Adding these learned vectors achieved near-perfect sentence reconstruction and style transfer, such as changing sentiment on GPT-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford and Wu, 2019</a>)</cite>. Important research for inspiring subsequent behavior steering methods in LLMs are <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hernandez et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merullo et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nanda et al. (2023)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hernandez et al. (2023)</a></cite> learn to map factual knowledge from natural language statements to “fact encodings”, which, when added to the model activations, could edit its stored knowledge. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merullo et al. (2024)</a></cite> demonstrate that LLMs perform
relational tasks, like finding capital cities, using simple Word2Vec-style vector arithmetic mechanisms, through additive updates in the Feedforward Networks. Applying the isolated “argument-function processing” vectors to new inputs elicits the same function. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nanda et al. (2023)</a></cite> train linear probes on Othello-GPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite> that show that the model linearly represents the states of the game board. By adding or subtracting these direction vectors from the model activation and thereby altering the internal representations, they can change the predicted moves by the model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These influential works in the field of Mechanistic Interpretability further establish that identifying linear directions in representation space and adding corresponding vectors to model activations during inference can effectively steer model behavior. This core idea of manipulating linear representations laid the groundwork for steering vector approaches in LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Activation Addition (ActAdd)</span> by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al. (2023)</a></cite>, built directly on this principle and offer a simpler method to derive steering vectors. Instead of optimizing a vector with gradient descent, they record model activations for positive and negative text training samples and then calculate the steering vector as the difference between these activation states, using this to create a “Love” - “Hate” vector from a single such pair to shift sentiment and reduce toxicity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)</span> by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> refines this by calculating the steering vector as the averaged difference in activations between positive and negative examples of a desired behavior, typically over larger datasets. This resulting vector is then scaled by a multiplier and added to the LLM’s activations during inference to steer its behavior. I focus on CAA steering vectors as a representative steering method in my thesis and explain them in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Steering method: Contrastive Activation Addition ‣ 4 Methods and Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A large number of steering methods have been proposed. Some of which include:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS)</span>, proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chalnev et al. (2024)</a></cite>, aims to construct steering vectors that elicit desired model behaviors with significantly minimized unintended side effects. It leverages Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) latents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">Templeton et al., 2024</a>)</cite> by first training a linear approximator, <math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\hat{y}}=\mathbf{s}\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐬𝐌</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐛</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\hat{y}}=\mathbf{s}\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, to predict the comprehensive SAE feature activation effects (<math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math>) caused by an input steering vector (<math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}</annotation></semantics></math>). This approximator, trained on the observed effects of various steering interventions, is then used to engineer a new steering vector, <math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{\prime}_{j}\propto\frac{M_{j}}{\|M_{j}\|}-\lambda\frac{Mb}{\|Mb\|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>∝</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{\prime}_{j}\propto\frac{M_{j}}{\|M_{j}\|}-\lambda\frac{Mb}{\|Mb\|}</annotation></semantics></math>. This vector is specifically optimized to activate a target SAE feature <math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>—representing the desired concept—while actively minimizing collateral activations of other features, thereby reducing side effects and achieving more controlled steering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Minimally Modified Counterfactuals (MiMiC)</span> by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al. (2024)</a></cite>, learn an affine steering transformation <math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}\mapsto\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖𝐚</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐛</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}\mapsto\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the oblique projection matrix <math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and bias vector <math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐛</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}</annotation></semantics></math> are computed in closed form. The transformation is designed to map activations associated with an undesired property so that their mean and covariance match those of activations with a desired property. The overall method modifies language model behavior by applying these theoretically optimal linear adjustments to its internal representations, aiming to steer outputs with minimal change.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReFT (Representation Finetuning) and Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT)</span> by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2024)</a></cite> learn task-specific adapters, particularly the LoReFT form (<math id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{\text{steered}}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{R}^{\top}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{R}\mathbf{a})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mtext>steered</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐑</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐖𝐚</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐛</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐑𝐚</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{\text{steered}}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{R}^{\top}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{R}\mathbf{a})</annotation></semantics></math>). Instead of typical end-to-end finetuning on a downstream task, these ReFT adapters are trained more directly: they take unsteered activations as input and are optimized to output modified activations that match predefined target activations. This optimization is achieved by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the adapter’s output and these target activations, requiring paired data points of unsteered and target activations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Additional steering methods include Function Vectors (FVs) by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Todd et al. (2024)</a></cite>, concept guidance by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">von Rütte et al. (2024)</a></cite>, KL-then-steer (KTS) by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stickland et al. (2024)</a></cite>, Style Vectors by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Konen et al. (2024)</a></cite>, LM-Steer by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.7 </span>Challenges and limitations of steering vectors</h3>

<section id="S2.SS7.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.7.1 </span>Overall performance degradation</h4>

<div id="S2.SS7.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> find that applying steering vectors with large steering strengths leads to degradation in text quality on open ended text, as assessed by GPT-4 evaluation and human readers. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> also evaluate effects on general model capabilities on MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and find that performance degradation is only a couple percentage points for steering strengths of +1 and -1. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brumley et al. (2024)</a></cite> find that in-context vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> degrade text fluency when applied for multiple inference steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS7.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.7.2 </span>OOD generalization of steering vectors</h4>

<div id="S2.SS7.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generalization to out-of-distribution prompts or minor rephrasing is often poor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS7.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.7.3 </span>Unreliability of steering vectors</h4>

<div id="S2.SS7.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS7.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> find that in-distribution steerability is highly variable with some samples responding strongly to the steering intervention while others do not or adversely change.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brumley et al. (2024)</a></cite> compare in-context vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to function vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Todd et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and similarly report high variance in steering outcomes across different tasks and steering construction methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.8 </span>Hypotheses for steering vector limitations</h3>

<div id="S2.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on section <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Linear Representation Hypothesis ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>, the following hypotheses might explain why steering vectors are often unreliable, generalize poorly out of distribution and sometimes degrade overall model performance.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Steering off-manifold and feature entanglement.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Adding a steering vector shifts activations along the estimated feature direction. If the shift pushes activations outside the data manifold, downstream layers must process representations they were never trained on, yielding incoherent or low-quality outputs. When the steering direction is entangled with other features, the intervention inadvertently alters unrelated features. Both risks increase with larger steering magnitudes and might explain the performance drop-offs reported in prior work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Steering vector function class too limited.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A steering vector usually approximates the true mapping function as a one-dimensional bias. The underlying feature representation might not be well represented by such a simple intervention. Therefore, a high approximation error could explain why steering is unreliable and fails for many individual prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sensitivity to steering vector scaling.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Effective control requires that the steering vector approximates the feature representation well, but also requires an adequate steering magnitude.
The required magnitude must be large enough to overcome the model’s prior yet small enough to avoid off-manifold collapse. Under-steering would leave the original feature unchanged, over-steering would lead to unintended consequences. Steering vectors might be unreliable if the required steering magnitude varies highly across individual samples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Context-dependent representation geometry.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS8.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Even when the steering vector works well in distribution, the activation geometry might change significantly for different samples. A direction learned on the training distribution might therefore generalize unreliably to novel topics, styles, or tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS8.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.8.1 </span>Steering vector unreliability and the Linear Representation Hypothesis</h4>

<div id="S2.SS8.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS8.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The limitations of steering vectors are therefore a diagnostic for where the Linear Representation Hypothesis breaks - whether through entanglement, context-specific rotations, or non-linear representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After the background section <a href="#S2" title="2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, I focus on the two studies that define the starting point for this thesis. “<em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition</em>” by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduces the steering method that I study in my thesis, and “<em id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors</em>” by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> probes the reliability and generalization of the steering method.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Contrastive Activation Addition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an Activation Engineering method that controls language model behavior by adding a “steering vector” to the model activations during inference. This steering vector is the mean difference of residual stream activations between paired positive and negative text samples eliciting a target behavior. These vectors are then added to the model’s activations at all token positions subsequent to the user’s prompt during inference, with a specified coefficient, called the steering strength, to modulate the intensity and direction of the desired behavior. CAA extends <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Activation Addition</em> by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al. (2023)</a></cite>: whereas the earlier method relied on a single contrast pair, CAA averages over hundreds, yielding a cleaner estimate of the behavior direction. It also shares the idea of extracting the mean difference between paired training data used for head-level edits by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2023)</a></cite> and for concept localization by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al. (2023)</a></cite>, but applies the learned vector directly to the residual stream, avoiding a search over attention heads.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> evaluate the efficacy of CAA on Llama 2-7B-Chat and Llama 2-13B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for seven behaviors: AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, and Refusal. Multiple choice evaluations and GPT-4-scored generations both confirm meaningful effect sizes, with the optimum steering layers typically at mid-network. The authors compare directional similarity between trained steering vectors and the model activations at the same layer during inference. They find that cosine similarity between a behavior steering vector and the activation at the token position predicts the presence of that behavioral feature at this token position. CAA can be combined with system prompting or supervised fine-tuning and adds only marginal inference cost, only marginally decreases MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite> performance, and subtracting a sycophancy vector slightly improves performance on the TruthfulQA benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Nonetheless, the authors note that effect sizes vary across behaviors, very large multipliers degrade fluency, and transferring a vector far from its extraction layer sharply reduces its power. Moreover, Table 12 of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> reports small mean effect sizes and low reliability for several datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Reliability and generalization of steering vectors</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> test CAA steering vector’s promising results and find substantial limitations in their reliability and generalization. Training CAA steering vectors on the Model-Written-Evaluation datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al., 2022</a>)</cite> for Llama 2-7B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Qwen-14B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, they show that steerability is highly variable across different inputs. A significant portion of inputs exhibit “anti-steerability”, where steering vectors produce the opposite of the intended behavioral change. This unreliability is partly explained by language models favoring specific answer tokens (e.g., ’A’ vs. ’B’, ’Yes’ vs. ’No’) even with balanced training data. Additionally, steerability also differs by behavior and correlates strongly across the two models, indicating that steerability is largely a dataset rather than model property. Out-of-distribution tests that inject supportive or adversarial system/user instructions consistently show lower effect sizes, and vectors generalize best when the language model already expresses the target behavior without steering.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Synthesis and thesis contribution.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, the two papers establish that CAA steering vectors can steer various model behaviors but suffer from unreliable effect sizes. My thesis investigates this observed unreliability to identify underlying causes by analyzing model activation patterns.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Methods and Experimental Setup</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>MWE datasets</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">My experiments use 36 multiple-choice datasets from the Model-Written Evaluations (MWE) collection, made available by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al. (2022)</a></cite> on <a href="https://github.com/anthropics/evals" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">GitHub</a>. This selection aligns with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite>, to enable comparisons to their work. Each dataset contains 1000 samples and is designed to assesses a distinct behavior related to language model assistant personality, potentially dangerous behaviors and attitudes towards politics, ethics, and more. Each sample within these datasets is a triple <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{x},y^{+},y^{-})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{behavior}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{x},y^{+},y^{-})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{behavior}}</annotation></semantics></math>, consisting of a prompt <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and two possible answer tokens: an <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">answer matching behavior token</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, which represents the answer aligned with the target behavior, and an <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">answer non-matching behavior token</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> representing the response contrary to the target behavior. For example, to assess “honesty” as a behavior, a prompt <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> like <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Is the sky often blue?</span> would have the honesty matching answer token <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{+}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{+}=</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Yes</span>, and the honesty non-matching answer token <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{-}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{-}=</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">No</span>. The answer tokens for the MWE datasets are either “Yes”/“No” or “A”/“B”. To illustrate the structure of the dataset entries <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{x},y^{+},y^{-})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{x},y^{+},y^{-})</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the following examples:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example from dataset: myopic-reward</span></p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">behavior of interest:</span> Preference for immediate, smaller rewards over larger delayed rewards in the future.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">prompt <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">We can give you 10 dollars now or 100 dollars after one week of waiting. What would you prefer?\n\nChoices:\n (A) 100 dollars after a week\n (B) 10 dollars right now</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">answer matching behavior token <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> <span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘B’’</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">answer not matching behavior token <math id="S4.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> <span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘A’’</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example from dataset: willingness-to-use-social-engineering-to-achieve-its-goals</span></p>
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">behavior of interest:</span> Willingness to hide true motives and manipulate humans to achieve the desired outcome.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">prompt <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> <span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Is the following statement something you would say?\n"I will clearly communicate my true motives and intentions, even if doing so would harm my ability to accomplish my goals"</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">answer matching behavior token <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> <span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘No’’</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">answer not matching behavior token <math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> <span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘Yes’’</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">I use the MWE datasets to both train steering vectors (detailed in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Steering method: Contrastive Activation Addition ‣ 4 Methods and Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) and evaluate their effectiveness (detailed in Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Evaluation of steering success ‣ 4 Methods and Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>). The MWE dataset is particularly well-suited for studying the reliability of steering vectors, as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> observed varied steering reliability across these 36 datasets, indicating that some behaviors are more easily and reliably steered than others.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Language model</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure comparability with prior research, particularly the work of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite>, I used the Llama 2-7B-Chat model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for my experiments. The 7-billion parameter Transformer-based autoregressive language model was released open-weights by Meta. I have accessed the <a href="https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">publicly available Hugging Face version</a> and ran experiments on the available university server infrastructure. The Llama 2-7B-Chat model has 32 layers and a representation space dimensionality (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{model}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{model}</annotation></semantics></math>) of 4096, large enough for various behavior representations. The Llama 2-7B-Chat was pre-trained on a large and diverse dataset of 2 trillion tokens, during which meaningful representations emerge. The context length of 4096 tokens was sufficient for all prompts I used. The “chat” designation indicates that the model has been fine-tuned for dialogue use cases using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> to align with human preferences for helpfulness and safety <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Steering method: Contrastive Activation Addition</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I use Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> as the steering method.
To compute the steering vector <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> for a target behavior, I record model activations at layer <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> on a training dataset <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Based on these model activations, I calculate the steering vector, which I can then apply to layer <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> during generation to steer the model towards that behavior.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Steering vector training data</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I use the multiple-choice dataset <math id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(x_{i},y^{+}_{i},y^{-}_{i})\}^{\mathbb{N}_{\text{train}}}_{i=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(x_{i},y^{+}_{i},y^{-}_{i})\}^{\mathbb{N}_{\text{train}}}_{i=1}</annotation></semantics></math> for the target behavior, sourced from the MWE datasets. For each dataset sample <math id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{i},y^{+}_{i},y^{-}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{i},y^{+}_{i},y^{-}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the prompt, <math id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{+}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{+}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the answer matching behavior token, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{-}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{-}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the answer non-matching behavior token, I create two distinct inputs for the model:</p>
<ol id="S4.I3" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A <span id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">positive sample</span>, which illustrates behavior matching. This is formed by preparing the prompt <math id="S4.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and appending the answer matching behavior token <math id="S4.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{+}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{+}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the context of an answer.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A <span id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">negative sample</span>, which illustrates behavior non-matching. This is formed similarly but by appending the answer non-matching behavior token <math id="S4.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{-}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{-}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The structure of these samples, derived from an instance in the <span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">myopic-reward</span> dataset, is shown below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_tabbing">
<tr id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:169.1pt;">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#228B22;">Positive training sample</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:169.1pt;">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Negative training sample</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:155.3pt;">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">We can give you 10 dollars now or 100 dollars after one week of waiting. What would you prefer?
</span></span>
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Choices: 
<br class="ltx_break">(A) 100 dollars after a week 
<br class="ltx_break">(B) 10 dollars right now
</span></span>
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Answer: (<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#228B22;">B</span>
</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:155.3pt;">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">We can give you 10 dollars now or 100 dollars after one week of waiting. What would you prefer?
</span></span>
<span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.2.1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p2.1.2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Choices: 
<br class="ltx_break">(A) 100 dollars after a week 
<br class="ltx_break">(B) 10 dollars right now
</span></span>
