</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This discussion synthesizes the empirical results from Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, arguing that the reliability of CAA vectors is not arbitrary but is determined by the underlying geometry of the model’s steering vector training activations. I demonstrate that reliable steering depends on two key properties: high “directional agreement” among the activation differences used for training the steering vector, and clear “separability” of the corresponding positive and negative activation clusters. When these conditions are met, the simple vector offset of CAA serves as an effective linear approximation of the target behavior and results in effective and reliable steering. Conversely, when directional agreement is low and activations are poorly separated, it suggests that the underlying behavior is not well-represented by a single, global steering direction. This geometric perspective reframes the problem, suggesting that unreliability stems from a fundamental mismatch between the simple, linear function class of CAA and the more complex representational structure of certain behaviors. To conclude this discussion, I situate my findings within the context of prior work and discuss the limitations of this thesis.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Interpretation of results</h3>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.1 </span>Directional agreement of the training activation differences</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I study how directional agreement, how well the training activation differences align with the resulting steering vector, impacts steering efficacy. I find that the directional agreement correlates with all measures of steering success.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">High directional agreement means that the steering vector direction effectively approximates the individual activation difference directions. High directional agreement also implies that individual activation difference directions are consistent between each other, so each approximates the target behavior representation similarly. This suggests that the target behavior representation itself is reliably linearly approximated by the activation differences and the steering vector. It is therefore intuitive, that such target behavior representations are also reliably steerable because the steering vector likely has a low approximation error for the theoretically optimal behavior transformation function that can transform a representation of the “negative” behavior into a representation of the “positive” representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Low direction agreement on the other hand means that the steering vector direction is not consistently aligned with the individual activation difference directions. Low directional agreement also implies that individual activation difference directions are not consistent between each other, so different training pairs elicit different representation directions for the same latent behavior representation. This suggests that the underlying latent behavior representation is not well approximated by the individual activation differences and the resulting steering vector. It makes sense that such a target behavior representation is therefore not reliably steerable by a CAA steering vector, which is a constant bias offset. This steering vector likely has a large approximation error to the theoretically optimal behavior transformation function that could transform a representation “negative” behavior into a representation of the “positive” behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.2 </span>Norm distribution of the training activation differences</h4>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Shape of L2 norm distribution</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Training activation difference norms ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (a) illustrates the distribution of raw L2 norms of the individual activation differences, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta^{l}(\mathbf{x}_{i},y^{+}_{i},y^{-}_{i})||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta^{l}(\mathbf{x}_{i},y^{+}_{i},y^{-}_{i})||</annotation></semantics></math>. Figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Training activation difference norms ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (c) plots the distribution of individual activation difference norms (<math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta^{l}_{i}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta^{l}_{i}||</annotation></semantics></math>) after normalizing by the mean of these individual norms (<math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E[||\Delta^{l}_{j}||]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E[||\Delta^{l}_{j}||]</annotation></semantics></math>) for each dataset. In both figures, the L2 norm distributions are approximately unimodal and symmetric, with a slightly positive skew across all datasets. The raw variance differs varies across datasets, with more steerable datasets tend to have slightly larger variance in absolute terms. When normalized by the dataset specific mean activation difference norm, the variance does not meaningfully differ. Because the bell-shaped distribution has a small variance relative to the absolute norms, choosing effective steering norms is predictable.
Steerable and less steerable datasets are not meaningfully differentiated by their distributional shape. Therefore, large variance in the activation differences or complex multi-modal distributions are empirically not the causes that some behaviors are unreliably steerable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Normalizing by the steering vector norm</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Training activation difference norms ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (b), datasets are visibly separated by their steerability rank along the x-axis. This distribution of individual activation difference norms <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta_{k}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta_{k}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math>, normalized by the norm of the steering vector <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math> for that dataset, reflects the results about directional agreement. This is because directional agreement influences the resulting steering vector norm, mathematically explained by Jensen’s inequality: The mean of this normalized distribution, which I denote as <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, can be expressed as:</p>
<table id="S6.Ex25" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S6.Ex25.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=E_{k}\left[\frac{||\Delta_{k}^{l}||}{||\mathbf{s}^{l}||}\right]=\frac{E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]}{||\mathbf{s}^{l}||}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=E_{k}\left[\frac{||\Delta_{k}^{l}||}{||\mathbf{s}^{l}||}\right]=\frac{E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]}{||\mathbf{s}^{l}||}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This holds assuming <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\mathbf{s}^{l}||\neq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\mathbf{s}^{l}||\neq 0</annotation></semantics></math>. The denominator, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math>, is a constant for a given dataset once the steering vector is computed. To understand the expected values of <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, I use Jensen’s inequality. The L2 norm, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{v})=||\mathbf{v}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{v})=||\mathbf{v}||</annotation></semantics></math>, is a convex function. For any random vector variable, such as <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{k}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{k}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, Jensen’s inequality states that <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E[f(\Delta_{k}^{l})]\geq f(E[\Delta_{k}^{l}])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E[f(\Delta_{k}^{l})]\geq f(E[\Delta_{k}^{l}])</annotation></semantics></math>. Applying this here: <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]\geq||E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]\geq||E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]||</annotation></semantics></math>
Given that the steering vector <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as the expectation <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]</annotation></semantics></math>, I can substitute this into the inequality:
<math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]\geq||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]\geq||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math>
From this, it directly follows that the mean <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> of the normalized distribution satisfies:</p>
<table id="S6.Ex26" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S6.Ex26.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\frac{E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]}{||\mathbf{s}^{l}||}\geq 1" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\frac{E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]}{||\mathbf{s}^{l}||}\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This mathematical result (<math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math>) provides the foundation for understanding how this normalization differentiates datasets. The degree to which <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds 1 is critically dependent on the directional agreement among the individual activation difference vectors <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{k}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{k}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When the individual activation difference <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{k}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{k}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> has high directional alignment for a particular dataset, the process of averaging these vectors to compute <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{l}=E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{l}=E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]</annotation></semantics></math> results in minimal “cancellation” of vector components. In such a scenario, the norm of the mean vector, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math>, will be close in value to the mean of the individual vector norms, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]</annotation></semantics></math>. In the limiting case where all <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{k}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{k}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> vectors are perfectly aligned, the equality <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]=||E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]||=||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]=||E_{k}[\Delta_{k}^{l}]||=||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math> holds. Consequently, for datasets exhibiting high directional agreement, the mean <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> of their normalized distribution will be close to 1. The empirical distribution of <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta_{k}^{l}||/||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta_{k}^{l}||/||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math> with the highest steerability are centered near 2 in Figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Training activation difference norms ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (b).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Conversely, datasets with the lowest steerability, have norm distributions with means larger than 4. Although L2 norms of individual activation differences <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta_{k}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta_{k}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math> are similar across datasets, the resulting steering vector norms differ widely. This is because of cancellation effects, when calculating the steering vector as the mean activation difference. For example, if two equally large vectors point in opposing directions, their individual norms are large, but the norm of their mean is zero. Directional disagreement leads to significant cancellation effects, which results in steering vectors <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> whose norm, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\mathbf{s}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\mathbf{s}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math>, is significantly smaller than the average of the individual norms, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{k}[||\Delta_{k}^{l}||]</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, this normalization scheme is expected to create a separation between datasets depending on their steerability.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.3 </span>Steering vector function class</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Section <a href="#S2.SS6" title="2.6 Steering methods ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a> I describe steering methods as mapping functions
<math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{behavior}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><mo rspace="0.108em" stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{behavior}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which should move an activation that encodes the negative behavior to one that encodes the positive behavior while preserving all unrelated information encoded within the activation. The key design choice is the function class <math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}</annotation></semantics></math> from which <math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{behavior}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{behavior}}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected during the training process. If <math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}</annotation></semantics></math> is too expressive, the estimator risks high estimation error, as numerous complex functions could fit the limited training data well but fail to generalize well both in and out of distribution due to overfitting. Conversely, if the function class is too restricted, the estimator incurs high approximation error as no member of the class can accurately approximate the required transformation. Motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis (Section <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Linear Representation Hypothesis ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>) CAA has a small class: one-dimensional bias offsets
<math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{behavior}}(\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{s},\qquad\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐬</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{behavior}}(\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{s},\qquad\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}.</annotation></semantics></math>
For this function class to approximate the latent behavior representations well and effectively steer model outputs, two empirical conditions should hold:</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">High directional alignment.</span>
The cosine similarity between the training activation differences <math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{l}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{l}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and the resulting steering <math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{s}}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{s}}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> should be high, implying that the estimated steering direction closely matches the individual activation differences, which approximate the latent behavior representation,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(ii)</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Narrow norm distribution.</span>
The L2 norms <math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta_{k}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta_{k}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math> should cluster tightly around their mean, so that a single steering strength <math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> can shift most activations by the required distance without overshooting or undershooting.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figures <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Training activation difference norms ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>(a–c) show that many behaviors violate exactly the first criterion: the directions of <math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{k}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{k}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> disagree, leading to substantial cancellation and a small steering vector norm.
By contrast, the variance of <math id="S6.SS1.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\Delta_{k}^{l}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\Delta_{k}^{l}||</annotation></semantics></math> is similar across steerable and unsteerable datasets, indicating that magnitude dispersion is not the main culprit. Reflecting on the hypothesis for unreliable steering outlined in section <a href="#S2.SS8" title="2.8 Hypotheses for steering vector limitations ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.8</span></a>, the unreliability seems to stem primarily from directional disagreement. CAA’s function class is often too inflexible to approximate latent behavior transformations that are not well captured by a single global direction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.4 </span>Separability along the difference-of-means line</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I find that separability of activations along the difference-of-means line is a reliable predictor of steerability.
Across the 36 MWE datasets, the discriminability index d’ computed on projected activations is significantly correlated with each of the steering metrics: the steerability rank, the mean per-sample effect size, and the fraction of anti-steerable samples (Fig.<a href="#S5.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ 5.5 Separability along the difference-of-means line predicts steerability ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>).
This relationship is intuitive because when positive and negative activations cluster around well-separated means (Fig.<a href="#S5.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 5.5 Separability along the difference-of-means line predicts steerability ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, top), a constant CAA offset can shift most negative samples across the class boundary. By contrast, when the two distributions overlap or exhibit large within-class variance (Fig. <a href="#S5.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 5.5 Separability along the difference-of-means line predicts steerability ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, bottom), any single offset mis-aligns a substantial portion of samples, limiting the attainable steerability.
The empirical link between d’ and steering success therefore supports the interpretation that better-differentiated representations of the target behavior and
its opposite make measurable change in behavior more likely after steering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ 5.5 Separability along the difference-of-means line predicts steerability ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows that d’ also correlates strongly with AUROC, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic, and the overlap coefficient, confirming that it captures the same notion of distributional separability. I prefer d’ because, unlike overlap-only measures, it additionally reflects the margin between non-overlapping distributions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS4.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agreement across other projection methods.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS4.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS4.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ 5.6 Separability along first LDA component and logistic regression direction ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> confirms that separability assessed on alternative linear directions, like the logistic regression weight vector and the first LDA component, correlates with the difference of means discriminability.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.5 </span>Impact of training prompt types on resulting steering vectors</h4>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Different prompts induce different vectors, but achieve similar outcomes.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I train separate steering vectors for each dataset and for seven prompt types using 250 training and 500 evaluation samples. Averaged across datasets, every prompt type yields a net-positive logit shift, and no prompt type consistently outperforms the others (Fig. <a href="#S5.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ 5.7 Effect of prompt types on steering vectors efficacy ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>). Steering performance is highly correlated across prompt types: datasets that are easy (or difficult) to steer with one prompt tend to be easy (or difficult) with all.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect-size variance remains large.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite similar means, all prompt types suffer substantial sample-level variability. Between 29% and 43% of evaluation samples move in the <em id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">opposite</em> direction (<span id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">anti-steerable</span> cases), and this fraction ranges from 3% to 50% on individual datasets (Fig. <a href="#S5.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ 5.7 Effect of prompt types on steering vectors efficacy ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>). Prompt variations that leverage in context learning to more effectively elicit the target behavior representation do not meaningfully improve the CAA steering vector unreliability identified by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompt types produce distinct directions in activation space.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although their macroscopic effects are similar, the steering vectors themselves do not directionally align. Pairwise cosine similarities between vectors trained on the same data but with different prompt templates span 0.07–0.86 (Fig. <a href="#S5.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ 5.7.1 Comparing steering vectors from different prompt types ‣ 5.7 Effect of prompt types on steering vectors efficacy ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>). Similar templates (e.g. <span id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prefilled-5-shot</span> vs. <span id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prefilled-instruction-5-shot</span>) cluster more tightly, while dissimilar templates (<span id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prefilled</span> vs. <span id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">instruction</span>) diverge. One straightforward explanation is that generating an answer token (A/B, Yes/No) and generating the token <em id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">after</em> the answer engage different internal representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS5.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These findings suggest that (i) different prompt types offer alternative linear approximations of the same nonlinear target behavior and (ii) the principal driver of steering reliability is the dataset’s underlying representation, not the prompt template. Prompt design can marginally influence the direction found, but cannot overcome cases where the behavior itself is poorly separated in the model’s latent space.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Comparison with related work</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">My empirical findings both confirm and refine the claims made by prior work on steering methods.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Variance of steering effect size.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">von Rütte et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Konen et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brumley et al. (2024)</a></cite>, I observe that</p>
<ul id="S6.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S6.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(i) steering vectors can achieve meaningful changes in model outputs on average for many behaviors</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(ii) there is large variance across samples, including cases in which the steering vector has the opposite of the intended effect</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(iii) the mean effect size and reliability vary across behaviors datasets, with some being more much steerable than others</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extending the unreliability analysis of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> observe differences of severability across datasets and attribute sample level variance mainly to a steerability bias arising from answer-token polarity. My directional-agreement analysis shows that this bias is one instance of a more general issue: whenever individual contrastive differences point in divergent directions, the mean-difference vector (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>) becomes a poor global approximation of the latent behavior representation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Clarifying the role of prompt engineering.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> reported that CAA performance degrades out of distribution, but did not isolate whether this is due to the prompt template itself or to deeper representational factors. By training seven vectors on distinct prompt types (Section <a href="#S5.SS7" title="5.7 Effect of prompt types on steering vectors efficacy ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.7</span></a>) I show that, although the learned directions can differ substantially, their behavioral effect sizes are highly correlated.
This supports the interpretation that prompt variations merely sample different linear approximations of the same latent behavior representation. The fundamental driver of unreliability is the latent representation, not the wording of the prompt.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Function-class perspective.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Framing steering methods as the choice of a function class <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}</annotation></semantics></math>(Section <a href="#S6.SS1.SSS3" title="6.1.3 Steering vector function class ‣ 6.1 Interpretation of results ‣ 6 Discussion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1.3</span></a>) provides a unifying lens for these results. Both the original CAA paper and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> implicitly work with a one-dimensional bias class. My experiments quantify the empirical conditions under which this class suffices (high directional agreement, narrow norm distribution) and when it does not (directional disagreement, unpredictable norm).
This analytic framing categorizes different steering methods by their function class <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>behavior</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{behavior}}</annotation></semantics></math> and motivates to select the methods with appropriate function classes that balance approximation and estimation error.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overall contribution in the context of the related work.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduce CAA steering vectors and demonstrate their efficacy across a range of datasets. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2024)</a></cite> then highlight large per-sample effect size variance and varying steering efficacy across datasets. My thesis investigates why this unreliability arises and why it differs substantially across datasets. By linking steerability to the geometric structure of the training activation differences, I provide an intuitive explanation, offer visualizations, and quantitative predictors that identify when the one-dimensional CAA function class is inadequate and a steering method with a larger function class is needed to effectively approximate the latent behavior representation</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Limitations</h3>

<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Breadth of experimental setup.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">My presented results are derived using the Llama 2-7B-Chat model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. (2023)</a></cite>, using CAA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>)</cite> as the steering method, and evaluating on the 36 multiple-choice MWE datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al. (2022)</a></cite> common in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
The discovered relationships between activation geometry and steerability may be specific to this experimental setup. Based on my own preliminary results on other models and datasets during the exploration phase of this thesis and results from prior work I anticipate that my results for CAA steering vectors will transfer to other transformer based language models and steering vector methods like Function Vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Todd et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and BiPO  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> that used linear offsets, but verifying this transfer would be helpful. On the other hand, generalization of my results to more expressive steering methods such as MiMiC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, ACE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marshall et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or LoREST <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krasheninnikov and Krueger, 2024</a>)</cite>, all of which involve projection matrices instead of just a shift by a constant vector is uncertain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Methodology for prompt type comparison.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Statistically comparing steering vectors trained on different prompt types is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like training-set size, complicating robust analysis.
With few (5–30) randomly sampled training activations, steering vectors for the same prompt type vary so widely that true differences between prompt types are lost in the intra prompt type variance. Conversely, when drawing many (200–500) training activations, the intra prompt type variance disappears (cosine similarity <math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;0.99" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;0.99</annotation></semantics></math>), making resampling redundant. While I could run enough subsampling to achieve statistical significance in both cases, I believe this would add little practical insight. The second issue is that I evaluate steering vectors computed using different prompt types on a test set with the “prefilled” prompt type used in prior works like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>).
This might unfairly benefit steering vectors trained using the same prompt type.
Rigorous testing under carefully chosen conditions is needed for stronger statistical conclusions from prompt type variations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Correlation vs. causation in steerability</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A more conceptual limitation lies in the correlational nature of my findings. I establish a strong predictive link between the directional agreement and separability of activations and the effectiveness of steering. My visualizations and explanations help explain this plausible relationship. However, this does not constitute definitive proof of a causal mechanism. A plausible hypothesis is that both observations are symptoms of a common underlying cause: the existence of a coherent, linear representation of the behavior within the model’s activation space. Proving this causality is a significant challenge, as it would require moving beyond the observational methods of this study to interventional experiments that could, for instance, control for and shape a model’s internal representations during training. Because it is currently not technically possible to identify or control the true latent behavior representation in a model, such experiments are not feasible.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<section id="S7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.1 </span>Summary of findings</h3>

<section id="S7.SS1.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">First research question</h4>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">What are the underlying factors in model activation patterns that contribute to the observed variability in CAA steering vector reliability across different datasets and target behaviors?</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Directional agreement</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(mean cosine similarity between individual training activation differences and the resulting steering vector) is a statistically significant predictor of steering success, as shown in Results <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Directional agreement predicts steerability ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>. Higher directional agreement correlates with larger mean effect sizes, fewer anti-steerable samples, and lower steerability ranks across all datasets. When training activation differences point in a coherent direction, the learned steering vector is an accurate linear approximation for the latent behavior representation. As discussed in Discussion <a href="#S6.SS1.SSS1" title="6.1.1 Directional agreement of the training activation differences ‣ 6.1 Interpretation of results ‣ 6 Discussion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1.1</span></a> adding the steering vector therefore shifts the activations more reliably towards the target behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Activation difference norms</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The distribution of individual activation difference magnitudes is approximately unimodal and symmetric across all datasets (see Figure <a href="#S5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 5.4 Training activation difference norms ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>(a–c)). This uniformity suggests that steering magnitudes do not need to match complex multimodal or high variance distributions to effectively change the state of the target behavior. Instead, the required steering strengths are predictable, and CAA steering unreliability is primarily caused by inconsistent direction and not inconsistent magnitude (see Discussion <a href="#S6.SS1.SSS2" title="6.1.2 Norm distribution of the training activation differences ‣ 6.1 Interpretation of results ‣ 6 Discussion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Separability along the difference-of-means line</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The discriminability index <math id="S7.SS1.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> between positive and negative activations projected onto the difference-of-means line also correlates significantly with all three steerability metrics (see Results <a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Separability along the difference-of-means line predicts steerability ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a>). Clear separation indicates that the model encodes the state of the target behavior by its position on the difference-of-means line. Therefore, shifting an activation along this direction is more likely to flip the model’s interpretation from “negative” to “positive”, or vice versa. When the two distributions overlap, the association between position on the difference-of-means line and likely model interpretation of the behavior state as “negative” or “positive” is less consistent. Therefore, a behavioral change is less likely when shifting activations along the steering direction (see Discussion <a href="#S6.SS1.SSS4" title="6.1.4 Separability along the difference-of-means line ‣ 6.1 Interpretation of results ‣ 6 Discussion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Second research question</h4>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Can the training process of CAA steering vectors be modified to produce more consistently reliable control over language model behavior?</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSSx2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Steering vector training prompt variations.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSSx2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Systematically varying the steering vector training prompts and leveraging in-context learning change the training activation differences. Each of the seven training prompt types results in a directionally different steering vector, but their steering performance correlates significantly across datasets. For all prompts, the mean effect size is net positive, but all suffer from high variance in their effect size (see Figure <a href="#S5.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ 5.7 Effect of prompt types on steering vectors efficacy ‣ 5 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>). These findings suggest that steering unreliability is primarily a property of the behavior representation itself and cannot be resolved by improved training data. Steerable behavior representations are sufficiently well approximated by linear steering directions for effective steering, irrespective of the training prompt used. Less steerable behavior representations appear to require more expressive non-linear or higher-rank interventions for reliable control (see Discussion <a href="#S6.SS1.SSS5" title="6.1.5 Impact of training prompt types on resulting steering vectors ‣ 6.1 Interpretation of results ‣ 6 Discussion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.2 </span>Future work</h3>

<section id="S7.SS2.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Extend analysis to other steering methods</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Different steering methods exhibit variable success across different behaviors and tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stickland et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brumley et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pres et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Visualizing and measuring directional agreement and separability along the steering transformation would likely help explain the variable reliability of different steering methods. Such research could further contribute to determine whether the unreliability of many steering methods is caused by a mismatch of the steering methods function class and a model’s internal representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Cross-architecture validation</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Replicate my findings across a larger range of models to establish the robustness of my findings across model sizes, training stages and architectural variations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSSx3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Predict steerability from descriptions of behaviors</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A long-term aspiration is to predict the steerability of a behavior or concept from a qualitative description alone. Such research would need to investigate which behaviors language models learn to represent in simple, linear representations, and which in more complex non-linear representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSSx4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Efficacy in open-ended generation</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSSx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSSx4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Steering methods are predominantly evaluated in multiple choice settings, while their efficacy in open-ended text generation remains understudied. Future work should focus on developing techniques to measure and steer behavior in open-ended text generation tasks. This will require creating evaluation metrics that go beyond logit differences to assess the holistic impact of steering on text quality, coherence, and unintended side effects.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSSx5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Hybrid control methods</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSSx5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSSx5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Combining steering vectors with prompt engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib106" title="" class="ltx_ref">Braun et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, modified decoding strategies and other methods for controlling text generation is promising and could offer improved trade-offs between control strength and text quality preservation over steering alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSSx6" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Multi-objective steering</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSSx6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSSx6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real-world deployments often require balancing several behavioral goals simultaneously. Investigating vector composition or constrained optimization could enable coherent multi-behavior steering while minimizing interference and text degradation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.3 </span>Concluding remarks</h3>

<div id="S7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">My thesis investigates when and why CAA steering vectors are unreliable. My findings validate intuitive geometric predictors of steering success with experiments and visualizations. First, I find that steering vector performance depends on how the target behavior is represented in the activation space. Both directional agreement of individual training activation differences and their separability along the steering direction are empirical predictors and conceptual intuitive explanations for steering vector unreliability.
Second, I find that different training prompt variations result in directionally different approximations for the same latent behavior representation. The resulting steering vectors however have similar overall performance and their steering effectiveness is correlated across datasets.
My findings suggest that steering vector reliability depends on whether the target behavior representation is well approximated by a linear steering direction. Unreliable behaviors consistently exhibit high directional disagreement and poor separability, a fundamental issue that persists even across different training prompt variations. These insights provide a clear diagnostic for CAA steering unreliability and a basis for developing more robust steering methods that account for non-linear representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_title">ReFT: representation finetuning for language models</span>.
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">In <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_inbook">The Thirty-eighth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems</span>,
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">External Links: <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_links"><a href="https://openreview.net/forum?id=fykjplMc0V" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_bib_external">Link</a></span>

</span></li>
<li id="bib.bib78" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_inproceedings"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Zeiler and Fergus (2014)</span>

</span></li>
<li id="bib.bib32" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_article"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Zou <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">et al.</span> (2023)</span>

</span>

</ul>
</section>

<div id="A1.SSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Die Konzeption, Implementierung, Durchführung und Auswertung aller in diesem Paper präsentierten Experimente erfolgte durch mich. Meine Koautoren unterstützten mich dabei durch wissenschaftliche Beratung und Feedback. Die initiale Fassung des Papers wurde ebenfalls von mir verfasst und anschließend in Kollaboration mit den Koautoren finalisiert. Die in dieser Abschlussarbeit dargestellten Inhalte basieren auf dieser Forschungsarbeit und vertiefen die entsprechenden Aspekte.</p>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Mathematical Notation</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Introduction to Transformers</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The transformer architecture was introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al. (2017)</a></cite>. The notation is inspired from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phuong and Hutter (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 1: Tokenization</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The input text is segmented into tokens <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> - which may be words, sub-words, or characters - using a tokenizer, often pre-trained on a large corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sennrich et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib105" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. These tokens form the model’s vocabulary <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>. Each token is mapped to a unique token ID <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in[\mathbb{N}_{V}]:=\{1,\ldots,\mathbb{N}_{V}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in[\mathbb{N}_{V}]:=\{1,\ldots,\mathbb{N}_{V}\}</annotation></semantics></math> from the model’s vocabulary, translating human-readable text into natural numbers <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, the word “cat” might be tokenized into the token ID 1777 using a tokenizer. This discrete representation enables the subsequent numerical processing performed by the model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 2: Token embedding</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Token IDs are mapped to fixed-size dense vector embeddings <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> in a high-dimensional representation space <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>. These embeddings, learned during training, encode semantic and syntactic properties of the tokens. For instance, token ID 1777 might be mapped to a vector <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.41,\ldots,0.97]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.41</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0.97</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.41,\ldots,0.97]</annotation></semantics></math>. This mapping from token IDs (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>) to vectors (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>) is done by an embedding matrix <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\mathbb{N}_{V}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\mathbb{N}_{V}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which effectively acts as a lookup table. Additionally, positional information is incorporated through the positional embedding matrix <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\tau_{\text{max}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}\times\tau_{\text{max}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 3: Transformations by the Transformer</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The initial embedding vector <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> is iteratively processed through multiple Transformer layers. Each layer applies attention mechanisms, non-linear activation functions, and layer normalization. The vector’s dimensionality <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> typically remains constant. Conceptually, each layer transforms its input vector by incorporating contextual information from other tokens in the sequence, capturing complex inter-token dependencies. This process results in a contextually enriched output vector <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 4: Prediction head</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prediction head converts the final contextual output vector <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> into a probability distribution over the model’s entire vocabulary <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>. This distribution signifies the likelihood of each token being the next in the sequence. For instance, an output vector <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1.17,\ldots,0.37]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>1.17</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0.37</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1.17,\ldots,0.37]</annotation></semantics></math> is passed through a linear layer and a softmax function to generate probabilities for tokens like “sleeps” or “jumps.” Mathematically, this transforms <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> via a linear projection with a weight matrix <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}_{V}\times d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}_{V}\times d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> to produce logits, which a softmax function then transforms into a probability distribution over the <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}_{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℕ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}_{V}</annotation></semantics></math> vocabulary tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Step 5: Sampling and token translation</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the generated probability distribution, a token ID is selected, often by choosing the most probable token (greedy decoding) or by employing other sampling strategies. This selected token ID is then converted back into its human-readable token representation. For example, if token ID 1998 is selected, it might correspond to the word “sleeps.” This stage maps the probability distribution over the vocabulary (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{|V|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{|V|}</annotation></semantics></math>) to a specific token ID (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>), which is subsequently translated into human-readable text. This mapping from the model’s internal numerical predictions back to human language completes one generation step. The generation steps can be repeated autoregressively, meaning the just-generated token is used as input to the model to help predict the subsequent token, allowing for the generation of entire sequences.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

<td id="A2.T2.3.68.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><math id="A2.T2.m90" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(\Delta m_{LD}(x_{i})&lt;0)\in\left[0,1\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\Delta m_{LD}(x_{i})&lt;0)\in\left[0,1\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A2.T2.3.68.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">fraction / probability of anti-steerable sample</td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
</section>

(2024)</a></cite>, I select 36 datasets from the 154 available in the Model-Written Evaluations (MWE) collection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al.
